subtopic_detail: Daily headache in a woman whose episodic migraine has become continuous while she takes a combination analgesic
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 34 year old woman who says her head has hurt on most days for the past six months. Two years ago she had one or two bad headaches a month with nausea and light sensitivity, each settling with a tablet. Now the pain is present when she wakes and is dull and pressing on both sides, with a severe throbbing attack roughly weekly.

She buys a combination tablet containing paracetamol, codeine and doxylamine over the counter and takes between fifteen and twenty doses a week, mostly because she is afraid a bad attack will start at work. She has tried no preventive medication. Her neurological examination including fundoscopy is normal and there is no neck stiffness, no new focal symptom and no headache that peaks within seconds.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72 per minute, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Fundoscopy normal, cranial nerves intact, no papilloedema, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Medication history: Paracetamol with codeine and doxylamine combination tablets, 15 to 20 doses per week for at least 6 months, no preventive agent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Add a sumatriptan tablet to be taken at the onset of every headache day she experiences
options.rationale: Adding a second acute agent to near daily analgesic use sustains the overuse pattern, and triptans themselves cause this syndrome at ten or more days per month. It would be reasonable only once acute use is back under about two days per week (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the brain and defer any treatment change until it reports
options.rationale: Imaging is indicated for red flags such as thunderclap onset, papilloedema, new deficit, immunosuppression or new headache after age 50, none of which she has. Delaying withdrawal while awaiting a scan prolongs the very exposure that is driving the pain (Source: RACGP: Headache in general practice).

options.text: Cease the codeine containing analgesic and start regular propranolol as daily prevention
options.rationale: Headache on 15 or more days a month with acute medication on 15 or more days for over three months in a known migraineur is medication overuse headache, and withdrawal of the offending drug is the treatment. Starting a preventive at the same time reduces the withdrawal headache and improves the chance of reverting to episodic migraine (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).
source_refs: International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition

options.text: Continue her current analgesia and begin amitriptyline at ten milligrams each night
options.rationale: Preventive medication started while the overused analgesic continues has a much lower response rate, because ongoing exposure maintains central sensitisation. Amitriptyline is a reasonable preventive choice but only alongside withdrawal (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Refer her for greater occipital nerve blocks before altering her regular analgesic intake
options.rationale: Nerve blocks are an adjunct used in specialist practice for refractory headache and do not address the daily codeine exposure that is generating the pattern. Referral first also delays the intervention with the largest effect (Source: RACGP: Headache in general practice).

explanation.summary: Medication overuse headache develops in people with an underlying primary headache disorder who take acute treatments too frequently, and it is one of the commonest reasons a previously episodic migraine becomes daily. Opioid and combination analgesics carry the highest risk and convert at around 10 days of use per month, while simple analgesics require about 15 days. Management is withdrawal of the overused agent, an explanation that headache will transiently worsen for one to two weeks, and simultaneous introduction of a preventive so the patient is not left without any plan. Most patients revert to their original episodic pattern within two months of withdrawal, which is also the diagnostic confirmation. Persistent daily headache beyond that point should prompt review for a second diagnosis.
key_points: Headache on 15 or more days per month plus acute medication overuse for more than three months in a known headache sufferer defines the syndrome
Opioid and combination analgesics trigger it at 10 or more days per month, simple analgesics at 15 or more
Withdrawal of the overused drug is the treatment, not addition of a second acute agent
Start a preventive at the time of withdrawal to cover the rebound period
Imaging is reserved for red flags, which are absent when the examination and fundoscopy are normal
explanation.pearls: Warn the patient that withdrawal headache peaks in the first three to seven days and settles within two weeks, because patients who are not warned almost always resume the tablets on about day four.

sources.label: International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition

subtopic_detail: Fourth episode of lower limb cellulitis in a year in a man with chronic lymphoedema
stem:
You are the registrar in a general medical clinic reviewing a 55 year old man two weeks after discharge from his fourth admission with right leg cellulitis in twelve months. Each episode has begun with rigors and a spreading red leg and each has settled on intravenous then oral flucloxacillin, and the current episode has fully resolved.

He has had chronic swelling of that leg since an inguinal lymph node dissection for melanoma six years ago and wears a compression garment inconsistently because it is uncomfortable in summer. Today the leg is swollen and firm but not red, warm or tender. Between his toes the skin is macerated and fissured with fine scaling. He has no ulcer, no diabetes and no injecting drug use, and his body mass index is 34 kg/m2.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76 per minute, blood pressure 132/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Non pitting oedema of the right leg with skin thickening, no erythema or tenderness, interdigital maceration and fissuring of the fourth web space, no ulceration
data_table.Investigations: C reactive protein 4 mg/L (less than 5), white cell count 7.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step to reduce further episodes?

options.text: Give a single intramuscular dose of benzathine benzylpenicillin now and repeat it if he relapses
options.rationale: Intermittent dosing given only around relapses does not maintain the continuous exposure that the prophylaxis evidence rests on, and this agent is used this way for streptococcal rheumatic fever prophylaxis rather than for cellulitis. Continuous oral therapy is the studied regimen here (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Start twice daily oral phenoxymethylpenicillin as continuing prophylaxis with review at twelve months
options.rationale: Two or more episodes of cellulitis in a year with a persistent predisposing factor such as lymphoedema is the trigger for long term antistreptococcal prophylaxis, which roughly halves recurrence while it is being taken. Treating the interdigital tinea and reinstating compression are essential adjuncts rather than alternatives (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
source_refs: PATCH I trial, New England Journal of Medicine

options.text: Treat the interdigital skin with a topical antifungal cream and take no other preventive measure
options.rationale: Clearing the web space removes an important portal of entry and must be done, but on its own it leaves the lymphoedema and the established recurrence pattern untreated. It would be sufficient only if this were a first episode without lymphoedema (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Refer for supervised compression bandaging and lymphoedema therapy as the only ongoing measure
options.rationale: Compression reduces limb volume and is part of the plan, but it does not by itself provide the antistreptococcal cover that recurrent disease with four episodes in a year warrants. Compression alone is appropriate where episodes are infrequent (Source: Australasian Lymphology Association: Position statement).

options.text: Prescribe a rotating cycle of oral doxycycline for one week in every month over the coming year
options.rationale: Pulsed broad spectrum therapy has no evidence base in this setting and selects resistance while leaving unprotected intervals. Doxycycline is reserved for suspected non multiresistant Staphylococcus aureus disease rather than routine streptococcal prophylaxis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Recurrent lower limb cellulitis is driven by a portal of entry, most often interdigital tinea or a fissure, acting on a limb with impaired lymphatic drainage, and each episode causes further lymphatic damage that raises the risk of the next. The prophylaxis evidence shows a clear reduction in recurrence while penicillin is being taken, with the benefit fading once it stops, so the decision is one of ongoing risk rather than a fixed course. Prophylaxis is offered when there have been two or more episodes in a year and a predisposing factor persists. It never replaces the other two limbs of management, which are eradicating the portal of entry and maintaining compression. Patients allergic to penicillin can use a macrolide for the same indication.
key_points: Two or more episodes in a year plus a persisting predisposing factor is the threshold for prophylaxis
Interdigital tinea is the commonest portal of entry and must be treated to make prophylaxis effective
Benefit is present while the antibiotic is taken and wanes after cessation, so review is scheduled rather than a stop date assumed
Compression therapy reduces limb volume and further episodes and belongs in the same plan
Absent erythema, normal C reactive protein and normal white cell count confirm this is prevention, not treatment of active infection
explanation.pearls: Look between the toes at every cellulitis review, because untreated tinea pedis is the single most modifiable portal of entry and topical terbinafine for two to four weeks clears most cases.

sources.label: PATCH I trial, New England Journal of Medicine

subtopic_detail: Positive immunochemical faecal occult blood test returned through the national screening program
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 62 year old woman who has brought in a letter reporting a positive result from the bowel screening kit she posted six weeks ago. She feels entirely well, her bowel habit is unchanged, and she has seen no blood in the toilet.

She has never had a colonoscopy. No first degree relative has had bowel cancer. She takes perindopril for hypertension and no antiplatelet or anticoagulant. On examination her abdomen is soft and non tender, and rectal examination reveals small external haemorrhoids that are not bleeding and no palpable mass. Her full blood examination shows haemoglobin 138 g/L (115-155) with mean cell volume 88 fL (80-100), and her ferritin is 96 micrograms/L (30-200).

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non tender, no mass, small non bleeding external haemorrhoids on rectal examination
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 138 g/L (115-155), mean cell volume 88 fL (80-100), ferritin 96 micrograms/L (30-200), immunochemical faecal occult blood test positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the immunochemical faecal occult blood test in three months and act only if it is positive again
options.rationale: A repeat test cannot lower the risk conferred by the first positive result and its false negative rate would falsely reassure both of you. Repeat testing belongs to the screening interval after a negative result, not after a positive one (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for colorectal cancer).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for colorectal cancer

options.text: Attribute the result to her haemorrhoids and review her again if she reports any rectal bleeding
options.rationale: Attributing a positive screening result to visible anal pathology is the commonest reason a colorectal cancer diagnosis is delayed, since haemorrhoids are present in a large share of this age group and coexist with neoplasia. Anorectal findings are only accepted as the explanation after the colon has been cleared (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for colorectal cancer).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for colorectal cancer

options.text: Refer her for colonoscopy with the aim of the procedure occurring within thirty days of the result
options.rationale: About one in twenty to thirty people with a positive screening test have a cancer and a further third have advanced adenomas, so colonoscopy is the required diagnostic step regardless of symptoms or a normal haemoglobin. Australian guidance sets a target of colonoscopy within 30 days of the positive result because longer delays are associated with more advanced disease at diagnosis (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for colorectal cancer).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for colorectal cancer

options.text: Order computed tomography colonography first and reserve colonoscopy for any abnormality it detects
options.rationale: Computed tomography colonography cannot biopsy or remove a lesion, so an abnormal study simply generates the colonoscopy that should have been done first. It is reserved for patients in whom colonoscopy is incomplete or unsafe (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for colorectal cancer).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for colorectal cancer

options.text: Send a faecal calprotectin level and base the decision to refer her on whether it is elevated
options.rationale: Faecal calprotectin measures mucosal inflammation to help separate inflammatory bowel disease from functional symptoms in younger patients, and a normal value does not exclude a colonic neoplasm. Using it here would introduce a test that cannot change the indication for colonoscopy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).

explanation.summary: The National Bowel Cancer Screening Program mails immunochemical faecal occult blood test kits to Australians in the eligible age range, and the entire benefit of the program depends on positive results proceeding to colonoscopy. Participation is good but follow up colonoscopy rates are not, and the largest avoidable harm in the pathway is a positive result attributed to haemorrhoids or a normal blood count. A normal haemoglobin and ferritin do not reduce the probability of neoplasia because intermittent bleeding from an adenoma or early cancer rarely causes anaemia. Colonoscopy also allows removal of adenomas, which is where the mortality reduction largely comes from. Surveillance intervals after the procedure are then set by the number, size and histology of anything found.
key_points: A positive screening test is a diagnostic indication for colonoscopy, not a reason to repeat the test
Roughly one in twenty to thirty positive tests reflect a cancer and about a third an advanced adenoma
Australian guidance targets colonoscopy within 30 days of the positive result
Normal haemoglobin, normal ferritin and visible haemorrhoids do not explain away the result
Computed tomography colonography is a fallback for incomplete or unsafe colonoscopy, not a triage test
explanation.pearls: Delay beyond about 120 days from a positive screening test to colonoscopy is associated with a measurably higher stage at diagnosis, which is why the 30 day target exists rather than a vague expression of urgency.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for colorectal cancer

subtopic_detail: Deciding the duration of anticoagulation three months after a first unprovoked proximal deep vein thrombosis
stem:
You are the registrar in a thrombosis clinic reviewing a 48 year old man three months after a first deep vein thrombosis involving the right femoral and popliteal veins. He has taken apixaban at treatment dose throughout and has had no bleeding, and his leg swelling has settled.

In the three months before it he had no surgery, immobilisation, plaster cast or long haul travel, and he has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism. Computed tomography of the chest, abdomen and pelvis at diagnosis and an age appropriate screening history revealed no malignancy. He is otherwise well, works as a plumber, drinks minimally, and takes no antiplatelet agent. His full blood examination, renal function and liver function are normal today, and his repeat ultrasound shows partial recanalisation with residual non occlusive thrombus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 68 per minute, blood pressure 126/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 148 g/L (130-175), platelets 232 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 78 micromol/L (60-110), estimated glomerular filtration rate greater than 90 mL/min/1.73m2, alanine aminotransferase 24 U/L (less than 40)
data_table.Imaging: Repeat compression ultrasound shows partial recanalisation with residual non occlusive thrombus in the femoral vein

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation plan from here?

options.text: Stop anticoagulation now on the basis that three months of treatment has been completed
options.rationale: Three months treats the index event but leaves an unprovoked clot with a recurrence risk of roughly 10 per cent in the first year and 30 per cent by five years. Stopping is the right choice when a major transient provoking factor such as recent surgery was present (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).

options.text: Continue apixaban indefinitely at the lower prophylactic dose with annual review of risk and bleeding
options.rationale: For an unprovoked proximal event in a patient with low bleeding risk, extended anticoagulation is recommended, and the reduced dose after the first six months preserves most of the reduction in recurrence with less bleeding than full treatment dosing. Extended therapy is indefinite with periodic reassessment rather than a fixed additional course (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism guidance

options.text: Change to low dose aspirin daily as ongoing secondary prevention against further clot
options.rationale: Aspirin reduces recurrence by about a third whereas extended low dose apixaban reduces it by around 80 per cent, so it is a distinctly weaker option here. Aspirin is reserved for patients who decline or cannot tolerate ongoing anticoagulation (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism guidance).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism guidance

options.text: Perform an inherited thrombophilia screen and let those results determine the treatment duration
options.rationale: Heritable thrombophilia results do not reliably alter recurrence risk enough to change the duration decision, which is already driven by the unprovoked nature of the event. Testing has a role mainly in selected antiphospholipid syndrome assessments where a positive result changes drug choice away from a direct oral agent (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism guidance).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism guidance

options.text: Switch to warfarin with a target range of 2.0 to 3.0 and plan to stop after six further months
options.rationale: Swapping a direct oral anticoagulant for warfarin adds monitoring and interactions without benefit in a patient with normal renal function and no antiphospholipid syndrome. A defined further course also misrepresents the risk, which does not fall away at a fixed end point (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).

explanation.summary: Duration of anticoagulation after venous thromboembolism is decided by whether the event was provoked and by bleeding risk, not by whether the clot has resolved on imaging. Events provoked by a major transient factor are treated for three months and stopped, whereas unprovoked proximal events carry a persistent recurrence risk that justifies extended therapy in patients who bleed rarely. Reduced dose apixaban or rivaroxaban after the initial treatment period retains most of the protective effect with a bleeding rate close to placebo in trial populations. Residual vein thrombus and D-dimer measured after cessation refine risk in research settings but do not replace the provoked versus unprovoked distinction. Every extended plan needs a scheduled reassessment because bleeding risk rises with age and comorbidity.
key_points: Provoked by a major transient factor means three months then stop; unprovoked usually means extended therapy
Extended therapy uses the reduced dose of apixaban or rivaroxaban after the first six months
Aspirin is markedly less effective than a reduced dose direct oral anticoagulant for this indication
Inherited thrombophilia testing rarely changes duration and is not routine
Extended means indefinite with review, not a second fixed course
explanation.pearls: Apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily started after six months of treatment dose therapy cut recurrent venous thromboembolism by about 80 per cent in the AMPLIFY-EXT trial with major bleeding no higher than placebo.

sources.label: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism guidance

subtopic_detail: Influenza confirmed on day two of illness in a frail aged care resident during a facility outbreak
stem:
You are the doctor attending a residential aged care facility where three residents have tested positive for influenza A in the past two days. You are asked to see an 82 year old woman who developed fever, a dry cough and aching limbs yesterday morning.

She has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with two exacerbations in the past year, uses tiotropium and a combination inhaler, and had her influenza vaccination four months ago. She is alert and orientated, her chest is quiet with a prolonged expiratory phase and no focal crackles, and her chest radiograph shows hyperinflation without consolidation. A point of care polymerase chain reaction swab taken this morning is positive for influenza A. Her creatinine is 96 micromol/L with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 48 mL/min/1.73m2.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 per minute, blood pressure 128/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 per minute, SpO2 93 per cent on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Influenza A detected on polymerase chain reaction, C reactive protein 42 mg/L (less than 5), white cell count 8.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), creatinine 96 micromol/L (45-90), estimated glomerular filtration rate 48 mL/min/1.73m2
data_table.Imaging: Chest radiograph shows hyperinflation with no consolidation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Start oral oseltamivir now at a dose reduced for her renal function and continue it for five days
options.rationale: She is in a high risk group by age, frailty and chronic lung disease, is within 48 hours of symptom onset, and has a laboratory confirmed infection, which is the clearest indication for a neuraminidase inhibitor. The dose is halved when the estimated glomerular filtration rate falls between 30 and 60 mL/min/1.73m2 (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Provide supportive care only because antiviral therapy has no benefit once fever is established
options.rationale: Benefit is greatest within 48 hours of onset and she is inside that window, so withholding therapy discards the intervention most likely to prevent progression in a frail resident. Supportive care alone is appropriate for a well younger adult presenting late (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Give oral amoxicillin for seven days on the basis of her fever and raised C reactive protein
options.rationale: A modest C reactive protein rise with no consolidation and a positive viral test does not support bacterial pneumonia, and antibacterial therapy would be added later if new focal signs or lobar consolidation emerged. This is the reflex that drives unnecessary antibiotic use in outbreak settings (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Prescribe inhaled zanamivir twice daily for five days as her preferred antiviral treatment option
options.rationale: The inhaled route risks bronchospasm and is avoided in people with obstructive airways disease, and it also demands an inspiratory effort that many frail residents cannot generate. It is an alternative where oseltamivir resistance is documented in someone without airways disease (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Await the formal laboratory confirmation of the subtype before committing her to any antiviral drug
options.rationale: Subtyping does not change the choice of a neuraminidase inhibitor and waiting would push her past the 48 hour window where treatment works best. Confirmatory subtyping matters for public health surveillance rather than for this treatment decision (Source: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Influenza guidelines).
source_refs: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Influenza guidelines

explanation.summary: Influenza in residential aged care spreads rapidly and carries a high case fatality rate, so both treatment and outbreak control decisions are made quickly and on clinical grounds supported by rapid testing. Neuraminidase inhibitors shorten illness modestly in healthy adults but are used in high risk groups to reduce complications, hospitalisation and death, with the benefit concentrated in the first 48 hours. Treatment is still offered beyond that window to severely unwell or hospitalised patients because viral shedding continues. Facility outbreaks also trigger antiviral prophylaxis for exposed residents, isolation of cases and exclusion of symptomatic staff, all coordinated with the public health unit. Vaccination earlier in the season reduces but does not eliminate risk, particularly when circulating strains have drifted.
key_points: Age, frailty and chronic lung disease place a patient in the high risk group where antivirals are recommended
Treatment works best within 48 hours of symptom onset and should not await formal subtyping
Oseltamivir dosing is halved when the estimated glomerular filtration rate is 30 to 60 mL/min/1.73m2
Inhaled zanamivir is avoided in obstructive airways disease because of bronchospasm risk
Recent vaccination does not exclude influenza when a strain mismatch or waning immunity is possible
explanation.pearls: In a declared aged care facility outbreak, oseltamivir prophylaxis is offered to exposed residents for at least ten days and continued until seven days after the last case onset, which is a separate decision from treating the index cases.

sources.label: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Influenza guidelines
